title: A Macro-Micro Assessment of Exchange Rate Shocks, Agricultural Prices and Household Welfare in Nigeria
content: The naira price of the US dollar rose by 67 per cent between May and July 2023. I ask how much of a shock of this kind reaches staple food and fuel prices, and whether it reaches households unevenly according to whether they buy or sell food. Local projections instrumented with Brent crude and three dated policy-shift months put cumulative pass-through to a staple food index at about 1.1 two months after the shock and 1.7 after twelve, and pass-through to a petrol price index at 0.9 to 1.0 after six to eight months. With only three policy episodes the instruments are weak (first-stage F of about 12 to 14), so I rely on Anderson-Rubin sets, which are wide. The petrol result depends on the June 2023 episode, which coincided with the removal of the petrol subsidy. I then turn the estimates into household-specific exposure, evaluated at each interview month, and link it to five waves of the Nigeria General Household Survey Panel (23,869 household-waves). Net sellers of food fare better: the interaction of exposure with net market surplus is 0.23 for real consumption (state-level wild cluster bootstrap p = 0.02). But exposure is close to zero in four of five waves, so the interaction mainly measures a shift in the net-seller gradient in the 2023/24 wave, and pre-trend checks do not isolate the exchange rate as its cause. I read the evidence as credible but imprecise pass-through estimates and a suggestive distributional pattern, and I set out the data that would settle the question.
